elements.quote: Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19, with this iteration synthesising relevant evidence up to June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly calls the work a 'living systematic review', identifying the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19, with this iteration synthesising relevant evidence up to June 7 th 2020.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective/topic of the review (suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19) and the time scope of this iteration.

elements.quote: Eligibility criteria include incidence/prevalence of suicidal behaviour, exposure-outcome relationships and effects of interventions in relation to the COVID-19 pandemic. Outcomes of interest are suicide, self-harm or attempted suicide and suicidal thoughts. No restrictions are placed on language or study type, except for single-person case reports.
elements.reason: The abstract lists included outcomes and key inclusion/exclusion constraints (no language/study-type restrictions except excluding single-person case reports).

elements.quote: this iteration synthesising relevant evidence up to June 7 th 2020. Method: Automated daily searches feed into a web-based database with screening and data extraction functionalities.
elements.reason: The abstract gives the date up to which evidence was synthesised and mentions automated daily searches, but it does not name the specific information sources/databases in the abstract text.
The abstract does not describe the methods used to assess risk of bias. Risk-of-bias tools (e.g. ROBINS) are described elsewhere in the manuscript but not in the abstract.

elements.quote: Our living systematic review (LSR) focuses on suicide prevention in relation to COVID-19, with this iteration synthesising relevant evidence up to June 7 th 2020. Method: Automated daily searches feed into a web-based database with screening and data extraction functionalities.
elements.reason: The abstract indicates that evidence was synthesised (and mentions automated searching and a web-based database), but it does not specify the methods used to present or synthesize results (e.g., narrative synthesis, thematic synthesis, meta-analysis).

elements.quote: Searches identified 2070 articles, 29 (28 studies) met our inclusion criteria, of which 14 articles were research letters or preprints awaiting peer review. All articles reported observational data: 12 cross-sectional; eight case series; five modelling; and three service utilisation studies.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of records retrieved and included studies and summarizes study designs, but it does not report the total number of participants.

elements.quote: No studies reported on changes in rates of suicidal behaviour. Case series were largely drawn from news reporting in low/middle income countries and factors associated with suicide included fear of infection, social isolation and economic concerns.
elements.reason: The abstract reports findings for the main outcomes (e.g., no studies reporting changes in rates; factors associated with suicide) but does not provide numbers of studies/participants per specific outcome or quantitative effect estimates.

elements.quote: We have not considered it appropriate to combine any results identified so far in a meta-analysis.
elements.reason: No meta-analysis was conducted; authors state it was not appropriate to combine results, so reporting a summary estimate is not applicable.

elements.quote: No studies reported on changes in rates of suicidal behaviour.
elements.reason: The abstract does not report comparisons between groups or direction of effect; no applicable group comparisons are presented in the abstract.

elements.quote: A marked improvement in the quality of design, methods, and reporting in future studies is needed. There is thus far no clear evidence of an increase in suicide, self-harm, suicidal behaviour, or suicidal thoughts associated with the pandemic. However, suicide data are challenging to collect in real time and economic effects are evolving.
elements.reason: The abstract briefly notes limitations regarding study quality, challenges in collecting suicide data in real time, and evolving economic effects, but it does not explicitly summarize standard limitations such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision in detail.

elements.quote: There is thus far no clear evidence of an increase in suicide, self-harm, suicidal behaviour, or suicidal thoughts associated with the pandemic. ... Our LSR will provide a regular synthesis of the most up-to-date research evidence to guide public health and clinical policy to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on suicide.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results (no clear evidence of increase) and states implications (the LSR will guide public health and clinical policy).
The abstract does not state the primary source of funding. Funding and grant acknowledgements appear elsewhere in the manuscript but are not reported in the abstract.
The abstract does not provide the register name or registration number. PROSPERO registration is reported in the Methods section but not in the abstract.

elements.quote: Given the health and economic threats posed by the pandemic to the global community, there are concerns that rates of suicide and suicidal behaviour may rise during and in its aftermath.
elements.reason: The abstract describes the current state (pandemic causing health/economic threats) and the important uncertainty (concern that suicide rates may rise).

elements.quote: Our LSR will provide a regular synthesis of the most up-to-date research evidence to guide public health and clinical policy to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 on suicide.
elements.reason: The abstract explains the importance and need for the review: to synthesise up-to-date evidence to guide policy and mitigation efforts.
No evidence was found describing existing similar systematic reviews or explaining the need for this review relative to prior reviews; no previous review is cited or discussed in the provided text.
Although eligibility included 'effects of interventions', the provided evidence contains no description of proposed mechanisms of action for any intervention.
No logic model or consideration of a logic model for complex interventions or delivery contexts is presented in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The overarching aim of the review is to identify and appraise any newly published evidence from around the world that assesses the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on suicide deaths, suicidal behaviours, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, or that assesses the effectiveness of strategies to reduce the risk of suicide deaths, suicidal behaviours, self-harm and suicidal thoughts, resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic.
elements.reason: The manuscript provides an explicit, overarching aim and clearly states the review questions/objectives (including both impact and effectiveness of strategies), fulfilling the requirement to state objectives/questions.

Although the review includes assessment of effectiveness of strategies, the retrieved evidence does not present planned intervention comparisons framed using PICO or an appropriate variant; no PICO-style planned comparisons are explicitly reported in the provided text.

elements.quote: Study participants may be adults or children of any ethnicities living in any country. Outcomes of interest are:  Deaths by suicide  Self-harm (intentional self-injury or self-poisoning regardless of motivation and intent) or attempted suicide (including hospital attendance and/or admission for these reasons)  Suicidal thoughts/ideation
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies participant characteristics, settings (any country), and detailed outcomes of interest and research questions/study types (see text_8 and callout_0). However, it does not explicitly state follow-up requirements or other detailed study eligibility features (e.g. minimum follow-up duration), so not all study-characteristic eligibility elements are fully specified.

elements.quote: No restrictions were placed on the types of study design eligible for inclusion, except for the exclusion of single-person case reports. Pre-prints were re-assessed at the time of publication and most current version included. There was no restriction on language of publication.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports eligibility criteria for report characteristics (study design restrictions, handling of pre-prints, and no language restriction), and gives the date range for the current iteration (Jan 1 to June 7, 2020) in the same section.
No explicit statement distinguishes exclusion because outcomes were not measured from exclusion because outcome results were not reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: We synthesised studies according to themes based on research questions and study design, using tables and narrative. Results were synthesised separately for studies in the general population, in health and social care staff and other at-risk occupations, and in vulnerable populations (e.g. people of older age or those with underlying conditions that predispose them to becoming severely ill or dying after contracting COVID-19).
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the groups used in synthesis (by theme/study design and specific population groups) and links these to the research questions/comparisons.

elements.quote: We did not include Google Trends studies (Jacobson et al., 2020; Knipe et al., 2020; Rana, 2020; Sinyor et al., 2020) since search data constitute a proxy measure but findings are largely mixed. We also excluded grey literature (Fancourt & Steptoe, 2020).
elements.reason: Rationales are provided for some notable restrictions (e.g. exclusion of Google Trends studies because search data are a proxy measure), but not for all restrictions (for example, exclusion of single-person case reports is stated elsewhere without an explicit rationale in the provided evidence), so the rationale coverage is incomplete.

elements.quote: A sample search strategy (for PubMed) appears in Box 1 from 1st Jan 2020 to June 7th 2020. ... Searches are conducted daily via PubMed and Scopus application programme interface and the bioRxiv and medRxiv RSS feeds. ... For this version of the living review, Psy- and SocArXiv searches were carried out retrospectively on the 12th of June, using a publication date filter for Jan 1st 2020 - June 7th 2020.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports explicit search dates (e.g. Jan 1 to June 7 2020), daily search frequency, and the retrospective PsyArXiv/SocArXiv search on 12 June, indicating dates when sources were last searched/consulted.

elements.quote: We searched the following electronic databases: PubMed; Scopus; medRxiv, bioRxiv; the COVID-19 Open Research Dataset (CORD-19) by Semantic Scholar and the Allen Institute for AI, which includes relevant records from Microsoft Academic, Elsevier, arXiv and PMC; and the WHO COVID-19 database. ... Searches are conducted daily via PubMed and Scopus application programme interface and the bioRxiv and medRxiv RSS feeds. A sample search strategy (for PubMed) appears in Box 1 from 1st Jan 2020 to June 7th 2020.
elements.reason: Database names and some platform/interface details (e.g. PubMed and Scopus via API; bioRxiv/medRxiv via RSS) are reported and PubMed coverage dates are given, but full platform/search-interface details and coverage dates are not provided for each database, so reporting is partial.

elements.quote: We searched the following electronic databases: ... medRxiv, bioRxiv; the COVID-19 Open Research Dataset (CORD-19) ... and the WHO COVID-19 database. ... For this version of the living review, Psy- and SocArXiv searches were carried out retrospectively on the 12th of June, using a publication date filter for Jan 1st 2020 - June 7th 2020.
elements.reason: Names of registers/repositories (CORD-19, WHO COVID-19 database, medRxiv, bioRxiv, PsyArXiv, SocArXiv) are given and date restrictions are reported for PsyArXiv/SocArXiv; however date restrictions are not reported for all listed registers/repositories, so the element is partially fulfilled.

elements.quote: The development version of the software for automated searching is available from Github: https://github.com/mcguinlu/COVID_ suicide_living. Archived source code at time of publication: http://doi.org/ 10.5281/zenodo.3871366 (McGuinness & Schmidt, 2020) License: MIT
elements.reason: A URL is provided for the project's GitHub (search code) and archived code, and the manuscript names online sources like the WHO COVID-19 database and CORD-19, but URLs for most searched websites/databases are not provided in the evidence, so reporting is partial.
There is no evidence that organisations or manufacturers were contacted to identify studies or that any such organisations were named.
No evidence describes types of individuals contacted to identify studies (e.g. experts, clinicians); this is not reported in the provided evidence.
The manuscript does not specify the types of reference lists examined (e.g. reference lists of included studies or of reviews) in the provided evidence.
There is no reporting of backward or forward citation searching details (seed reports, citation index/platform, or search date) in the provided evidence.
No details are provided about consulting journals or conference proceedings (names, dates covered, search methods) in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: A two-stage screening process was undertaken to identify studies meeting the eligibility criteria. First, two authors (either CO or EE) assessed citations from the searches and identified potentially relevant titles and abstracts. Second, either DG, AJ or RW assessed the full texts of potentially eligible studies to identify studies to be included in the review.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of reviewers for each screening stage: two reviewers for title/abstract screening and a single named reviewer (one of DG, AJ or RW) for full-text assessment.
The text describes who conducted each screening stage but does not state whether reviewers worked independently at any stage.

elements.quote: Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and where this failed, by referral to a third reviewer (KH, NK or PM).
elements.reason: The manuscript provides a clear process for resolving screening/data extraction disagreements, including escalation to a third reviewer when discussion fails.
No information is provided on processes used to obtain or confirm eligibility information from study investigators.

elements.quote: There was no restriction on language of publication. We will draw on a combination of internet-based translation systems and network of colleagues to translate evidence in a language other than English.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the methods to translate non-English abstracts/articles (internet-based translation systems and a network of colleagues).

elements.quote: We have developed a workflow that automates daily searches of these databases, and the code supporting this process can be found at https://github.com/mcguinlu/COVID_suicide_living. Searches are conducted daily via PubMed and Scopus application programme interface and the bioRxiv and medRxiv RSS feeds... The software includes a systematic search function based on regular expressions to search results retrieved from the WHO, CORD-19 and preprint repositories (search strategy available in extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes automation tools integrated into the selection process (automated daily searches, code repository, conversion scripts, and a software search function).
There is no mention of externally derived classifiers by version or reference, their role, or records removed before screening.
No information is provided about internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use.
The manuscript does not describe use of machine-learning prioritisation tools or any stopping/prioritisation rules for screening.
No crowdsourcing platforms or their integration into study selection are described.

There is no description that previously screened datasets were used to eliminate records; underlying data mention a screening snapshot but do not describe using prior screened datasets to remove records.

elements.quote: One author (DG, AJ or RW) extracted data from each included study using a piloted data extraction form (see extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)), and the extracted data were checked by one other author (AJ, or EE where AJ extracted data).
elements.reason: States that one author extracted data from each study and that extracted data were checked by another author, indicating two reviewers were involved in data collection/verification for each report.

elements.quote: One author (DG, AJ or RW) extracted data from each included study using a piloted data extraction form (see extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)), and the extracted data were checked by one other author (AJ, or EE where AJ extracted data).
elements.reason: Indicates multiple people were involved in extraction and checking, but does not explicitly state whether the multiple data collectors worked independently.

elements.quote: Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and where this failed, by referral to a third reviewer (KH, NK or PM).
elements.reason: Provides the process for resolving disagreements: discussion and referral to a third reviewer if needed.
No information provided in the retrieved evidence about processes used to obtain or confirm data from study investigators.

elements.quote: We have developed a workflow that automates daily searches of these databases, and the code supporting this process can be found at https://github.com/mcguinlu/COVID_suicide_living. Searches are conducted daily via PubMed and Scopus application programme interface and the bioRxiv and medRxiv RSS feeds. Conversion scripts for the daily updated WHO and the weekly updated CORD-19 corpus are used to collect information from the remaining sources. The software includes a systematic search function based on regular expressions to search results retrieved from the WHO, CORD-19 and preprint repositories (search strategy available in extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)). The platform allowed for data extraction via a built-in form.
elements.reason: Describes automation tools and scripts used for searching and a custom platform with a built-in data extraction form, but does not report details on training or validation of these automation tools.

elements.quote: There was no restriction on language of publication. We will draw on a combination of internet-based translation systems and network of colleagues to translate evidence in a language other than English.
elements.reason: Specifies methods to translate articles: internet-based translation systems and a network of colleagues.
No information in the retrieved evidence about any software used to extract data from figures.
No decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports or for resolving inconsistencies between multiple reports are described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: Two of the eight case series focused on suicide attempts and six on suicide deaths. Of the 12 independent cross-sectional surveys ten assessed suicidal thoughts of which two also assessed suicide attempts ... A range of validated questionnairres were used to assess suicidal thoughts.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists outcome domains assessed in included studies (suicide attempts, suicide deaths, suicidal thoughts) and describes the measures used to assess them.

elements.quote: Four used the question 9 single item from PHQ-9 'Have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself in some way' with four levels of response ranging from 'not at all' to 'nearly every day' over the last 2 weeks. ... the WHO Self Reporting Questionnaire (with one item of 20 asking 'Has the thought of ending your life been on your mind?', response yes/no in the last 30 days) ... Two studies used the Self-injurous Thoughts and Behaviours Interview (SITBI) to assess for presence ( yes / no ) of active suicidal thoughts (i.e., 'Have you had thoughts of killing yourself?') in the past month ... Ammerman et al . (2020) used one adapted item from the SITBI 'In the past month, have you attempted to kill yourself?' ( yes/no ) ... Table 5: Outcome: 9th Thoughts of self-harm in the last 7 days from the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression (EPDS...)
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the measurement time frames used in the included studies (e.g. last 2 weeks, last 7 days, past month, last 30 days) for outcomes such as suicidal thoughts and attempts.
No statement was found indicating whether the review sought all results compatible with each outcome domain (e.g. all measures, time points, analyses) across studies.
There is no description of a process used to select among multiple compatible results within outcome domains (e.g. prioritisation rules) when not all results were sought.

elements.quote: Since publication of our protocol we have amended our methodology to: 1) search additionally the PsyArXiv and SocArXiv open access paper repositories; 2) include modelling studies within the scope of our review (e.g. to predict the likely impact of the pandemic on suicide rates); and 3) update our research questions to include adult self-neglect and parental neglect and fear of losing livelihood.
elements.reason: No changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance are reported in the provided evidence; only methodological scope and research question amendments are described, so reporting of outcome-domain changes does not apply based on available text.

elements.quote: Irrespective of study design, data source and outcome measure examined, the following basic data were extracted: citation; study aims and objectives; country/setting; characteristics of participants; methods; outcome measures (related to self-harm / suicidal behaviour and COVID-19); key findings; strengths and limitations; reviewer's notes.
elements.reason: No changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains are reported in the provided evidence; data extraction process is described but no amendments to selection processes are indicated, so this conditional item does not apply here.
The manuscript does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting the review's conclusions nor provide a rationale for any prioritisation.

elements.quote: Irrespective of study design, data source and outcome measure examined, the following basic data were extracted: citation; study aims and objectives; country/setting; characteristics of participants; methods; outcome measures (related to self-harm / suicidal behaviour and COVID-19); key findings; strengths and limitations; reviewer's notes.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the other variables/data items that were sought and extracted for each study.
No explicit description was found in the provided evidence of assumptions made about missing or unclear study information.

elements.quote: One author (DG, AJ or RW) extracted data from each included study using a piloted data extraction form (see extended data (John & Schmidt, 2020)), and the extracted data were checked by one other author ... For articles where causal inferences are made ... we used a suitable version of the ROBINS-I or ROBINS-E tool to assess risk of bias as appropriate based on the research question and study design (Morgan et al., 2017; Sterne et al., 2016).
elements.reason: The manuscript cites a piloted data extraction form (with extended data reference) as the tool used for data collection decisions and cites ROBINS-I/ROBINS-E for risk-of-bias assessment.

elements.quote: "for causal inferences ... we used a suitable version of the ROBINS-I or ROBINS-E tool to assess risk of bias as appropriate based on the research question and study design (Morgan et al., 2017; Sterne et al., 2016)."
elements.reason: The manuscript names the risk-of-bias tools (ROBINS-I and ROBINS-E) and cites sources, but does not specify the exact version(s) used or provide version numbers or detailed identification of which version was applied.
No text in the provided evidence lists the specific domains, components, or items assessed by the risk-of-bias tool(s).
There is no information stating whether an overall risk-of-bias judgement was made for studies or the rules used to derive any overall judgement.
No adaptations to existing risk-of-bias tools are described in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: "we used a suitable version of the ROBINS-I or ROBINS-E tool to assess risk of bias ..."
elements.reason: The review reports use of established tools (ROBINS-I/ROBINS-E); there is no indication a newly developed risk-of-bias tool was created, so this conditional item does not apply.

elements.quote: "One author (DG, AJ or RW) extracted data from each included study ..., and the extracted data were checked by one other author (AJ, or EE where AJ extracted data). Disagreements were resolved through discussion, and where this failed, by referral to a third reviewer (KH, NK or PM). ... A two-stage screening process ... First, two authors (either CO or EE) assessed citations ... Second, either DG, AJ or RW assessed the full texts ..."
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies how many reviewers performed extraction and checking, indicates which roles were independent checks, and describes the process for resolving disagreements (discussion, then third reviewer).
No information is provided about contacting study investigators or processes used to obtain or confirm risk-of-bias information from study authors.

Although automation is described for search and screening workflows, there is no description of automation tools being used specifically for risk-of-bias assessment, nor details of their use, training, performance, or validation.

The Methods describe narrative synthesis and consideration of meta-analysis but do not specify, for each outcome or outcome type, which effect measure(s) (e.g. risk ratio, mean difference, OR) will be used in synthesis or presentation. (Evidence shows: "We synthesised studies according to themes based on research questions and study design, using tables and narrative... Where multiple studies addressed the same research questions, we assessed whether meta-analysis is appropriate... The current document is the first iteration of our review. We have not considered it appropriate to combine any results identified so far in a meta-analysis.") (chunk_id: callout_0).
No report of thresholds or ranges used to interpret effect size (or rationale) for outcomes was found in the Methods or elsewhere in the provided evidence.
No methods describing re-expression of synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g. converting ORs to risk ratios) were reported in the available methods text.

The choice of effect measure is not justified in the Methods or elsewhere in the retrieved evidence; the document describes synthesis approach but does not justify selecting particular effect measures for outcomes.

elements.quote: Data synthesis We synthesised studies according to themes based on research questions and study design, using tables and narrative. Results were synthesised separately for studies in the general population, in health and social care staff and other at-risk occupations, and in vulnerable populations (e.g. people of older age or those with underlying conditions that predispose them to becoming severely ill or dying after contracting COVID-19). Where multiple studies addressed the same research questions, we assessed whether meta-analysis is appropriate and would conduct it where suitable, following standard guidance available in the Cochrane Handbook (Deeks et al., 2019). The current document is the first iteration of our review. We have not considered it appropriate to combine any results identified so far in a meta-analysis.

elements.quote: To date, there is little literature exploring COVID-19 and suicide deaths, suicidal behaviours, self-harm and suicidal thoughts and most of the published evidence that we identified had important limitations. Importantly, much of the literature is not yet peer reviewed so the quality of reported studies may change. There were eight research letters, five pre-prints and for many others very short timeframes between submission and acceptance. All included studies were observational in design and prone to multiple sources of bias (eg, recall bias, selection bias, confounding). No conclusions can be drawn regarding causality and temporality from cross sectional studies. However, such study designs may be appropriate in current circumstances where timeliness of studies to inform policy and practice are important. However many were carried out too quickly and too early (one to two weeks post lockdown) in the outbreak to make meaningful contributions to the evidence base. The lack of baseline data in the majority of surveys included in the review and adjustments made to standardised measures to assess suicidal behaviours as well as the range of measures and timing asked made assessment of findings problematic.
elements.reason: The Extended Data 'Strengths And Limitations' explicitly describes multiple limitations of the included evidence (limited literature, many non–peer-reviewed reports, study designs observational and prone to bias, inability to infer causality, short timeframes, lack of baseline data and measurement issues), directly addressing the checklist requirement.
